overview: This file documents a 1932–1933 dispute over Japanese fishing vessels registered in colonial Taiwan that entered Philippine waters for fishing, small-scale trade, and the collection of natural resources. It begins with Taiwan’s licensing, tonnage, marking, logbook, and crew-qualification regulations for vessels operating south of 21° north latitude, then follows Philippine Governor-General Theodore Roosevelt Jr.’s objection that the rule could imply an incorrect northern boundary for the Philippines, whose islands extended to approximately 21°25′ north. State, War, consular, Philippine, and Taiwan officials exchanged reports and instructions, while a confidential Philippine assessment described a decade of incursions, illicit activity, arrests, escapes, and inadequate patrol capacity. Taiwan declined to amend the latitude in the regulation but circulated a clarification that Yami and North Island belonged to the Philippines and that the regulation did not authorize fishing in foreign territorial waters.

people.name: Frank LeJ. Parker
people.role: Brigadier General and Chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs, War Department

people.name: Stanley K. Hornbeck
people.role: Chief of the State Department’s Far Eastern Division

subfiles.title: Ketcham reports Taiwan’s controls on fishing vessels
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.to: Theodore Roosevelt Jr., Governor-General of the Philippine Islands
subfiles.about: Reports new Taiwan regulations intended to control Japanese fishing vessels operating south of the island and reduce incursions into Philippine waters.
subfiles.summary: Ketcham explains that complaints about Taiwan-registered boats entering Philippine waters had prompted discussions among Japanese, Philippine, and Taiwan authorities. The regulations require licenses, a minimum tonnage, conspicuous hull markings, operational logbooks, and qualified officers for motor fishing craft operating south of 21° north latitude. He expects these requirements to reduce violations and help Philippine customs officers identify offending boats.

subfiles.title: War Department transmits Philippine fishing correspondence
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary of War
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards Philippine correspondence concerning Japanese efforts to prevent fishing boats from entering Philippine waters illegally.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Secretary of War transmits Governor-General Roosevelt’s October 4 letter, Ketcham’s August 19 report, and Roosevelt’s August 26 acknowledgment. He particularly calls the State Department’s attention to the boundary issue raised in the third paragraph of Roosevelt’s letter.

subfiles.title: Roosevelt challenges the 21° licensing line
subfiles.from: Theodore Roosevelt Jr., Governor-General of the Philippine Islands
subfiles.to: Frank LeJ. Parker, Chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs
subfiles.about: Requests correction of Taiwan’s fishing order because the 21° line could be mistaken for the Philippines’ northern boundary.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt states that the 1898 peace treaty and the United States Coast Pilot place the northern Philippine limit in the Bashi Channel at approximately 21°25′ north. This boundary includes Y'ami and North Island in the Batanes group. He asks that Taiwan’s order be made applicable to waters south of 21°25′ rather than 21°.

subfiles.title: Enclosure copy of Ketcham report with Roosevelt’s acknowledgment
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, with appended acknowledgment from Theodore Roosevelt Jr.
subfiles.to: Theodore Roosevelt Jr.; acknowledgment to John B. Ketcham
subfiles.about: Reproduces Ketcham’s report on Taiwan’s fishing controls and appends Roosevelt’s August 26 acknowledgment.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure repeats the licensing, tonnage, marking, logbook, and officer requirements imposed on Taiwan-registered fishing craft operating south of 21° north. It links those measures to repeated incursions, suspected illegal fishing and trade, marine accidents, and diplomatic friction. In the appended August 26 acknowledgment, Roosevelt welcomes the measures as a material contribution toward solving the problem.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on three draft communications
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: William R. Castle Jr.
subfiles.about: Reviews draft communications concerning whether the United States should seek correction of Taiwan’s fishing order.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum finds the three outgoing drafts formally satisfactory. It nevertheless advises that the decision to act should be made without a recommendation from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.

subfiles.title: Stimson informs Hurley of instructions to Taihoku
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Patrick J. Hurley, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Confirms that the American consul at Taihoku has been directed to seek recognition of the 21°25′ Philippine boundary.
subfiles.summary: Stimson acknowledges the War Department’s November 7 transmittal. He reports that Ketcham has been instructed to raise the matter with the Government-General of Taiwan and promises to inform Hurley of subsequent developments.

subfiles.title: State Department informs Ambassador Grew
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Sends Ambassador Grew a copy of the instruction directing the Taihoku consul to address the disputed latitude.
subfiles.summary: The State Department encloses its instruction to Ketcham concerning Taiwan’s regulation of Japanese fishing vessels in Philippine waters. Grew’s attention is also drawn to Ketcham’s August 19 communication, already understood to be in the embassy’s files.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Ketcham to seek correction of Order No. 33
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John B. Ketcham, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Directs Ketcham to ask Taiwan authorities discreetly to move the licensing limit from 21° to 21°25′ north.
subfiles.summary: Ketcham is instructed to present the Philippine governor-general’s geographical evidence informally and discreetly. He is to request correction of General Order No. 33 so that it applies south of the asserted northern Philippine boundary and to report the results promptly.

subfiles.title: Parker transmits Roosevelt’s report on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: Frank LeJ. Parker, Chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Far Eastern Division
subfiles.about: Forwards a confidential Philippine report addressing sensational press accounts of Japanese activity and vessel incursions.
subfiles.summary: Parker supplies Hornbeck with Roosevelt’s August 15 response to questions prompted by American newspaper reports about alleged Japanese activity in the Philippines. He asks that the report be treated as information rather than as a formal request for State Department action. The document is present in duplicate.

subfiles.title: Roosevelt’s confidential report on Japanese boat incursions
subfiles.from: Theodore Roosevelt Jr., Governor-General of the Philippine Islands
subfiles.to: Frank LeJ. Parker, Chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs
subfiles.about: Assesses the frequency, purposes, and enforcement problems associated with Taiwan-registered Japanese boats entering Philippine waters.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt reports frequent incursions over at least a decade, especially around the Batanes and Babuyan Islands, with other cases in the Visayas and near Cagayan de Sulu. Investigations found intentional visits involving unlicensed fishing, small illicit trades, turtle and seaweed collection, shell gathering, rattan cutting, and removal of valuable timber; two detained crews escaped custody. Because northern waters were rough, islands sparsely populated, and patrol vessels scarce, he considered complete prevention impossible, though Philippine patrols and Japanese cooperation offered partial remedies. He also rejects rumors of broader governmental activity as unsupported.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledges Parker’s confidential information
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.to: Frank LeJ. Parker
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Roosevelt’s report and its restriction to informational use.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck states that Parker’s letter and Roosevelt’s August 15 account are of interest. He specifically notes both Parker’s request concerning treatment of the material and Roosevelt’s concluding assessment that no immediate official action was warranted.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs synopsis of Taihoku despatch No. 46
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Internal State Department circulation
subfiles.about: Summarizes Ketcham’s initial approach to Taiwan officials about the disputed latitude.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that Ketcham had conveyed the Philippine request to change the apparent boundary reference from 21° to 21°25′. Taiwan’s administration promised to examine the issue, although consultation with Tokyo might be necessary because Tokyo had participated in preparing the original order.

subfiles.title: Ketcham reports initial interview with Hiratsuka
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports presenting the Philippine boundary request to Taiwan’s Director General of Administration.
subfiles.summary: Ketcham explains that Hiratsuka’s absence in Tokyo and the Christmas and New Year holidays delayed the interview. On January 4 he described the actual northern boundary and transmitted the request to amend General Order No. 33. Hiratsuka promised to investigate, but Ketcham expected further delay because Tokyo’s approval would probably be required.

subfiles.title: Stimson updates Hurley on Ketcham’s initial approach
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Patrick J. Hurley, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Forwards despatch No. 46 and reports that Taiwan authorities are considering the Philippine boundary question.
subfiles.summary: Stimson supplements his November correspondence by enclosing Ketcham’s January 4 despatch. He notes that the facts were presented to Taiwan’s Director General of Administration, who agreed to investigate and inform the consulate of the government-general’s decision. The State Department promises further updates.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs synopsis of Taihoku despatch No. 53
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Internal State Department circulation
subfiles.about: Assesses Taiwan’s circular clarification as a practical recognition of the true Philippine boundary despite refusal to amend the order.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports that Taiwan notified relevant Japanese officials that 21° was a licensing limit rather than a definition of the Philippine boundary. The notification expressly recognized that Philippine islands lay north of that latitude. Although short of full compliance with the Department’s instruction, the result was considered sufficient to correct any official misunderstanding.

subfiles.title: Ketcham reports negotiated clarification of Order No. 33
subfiles.from: John B. Ketcham, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.to: U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports Taiwan’s refusal to amend its fishing order and its agreement instead to warn officials that Philippine islands lay north of 21°.
subfiles.summary: After several interviews with productive-industries and fisheries officials, Ketcham found Taiwan unwilling to concede that the Philippine boundary had influenced the regulation. Officials maintained that the order concerned shipwreck prevention and international disputes and declined to define a foreign boundary or amend the text. Ketcham secured a compromise circular identifying Yami and North Island as Philippine territory north of 21° and clarifying that the regulation did not apply within another country’s territorial waters.

subfiles.title: Kohama notifies Ketcham that governors received the clarification
subfiles.from: Kiyokane Kohama, Acting Director General of Administration
subfiles.to: John B. Ketcham, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.about: Confirms that Taiwan’s local governors were sent a notice clarifying the fishing-control regulation.
subfiles.summary: Kohama responds to Ketcham’s proposal regarding fishing controls. He states succinctly that local governors have been notified and encloses a copy of the notice.

subfiles.title: Taiwan circular on motor fishing vessels and Philippine islands
subfiles.from: Kiyokane Kohama, Acting Director General of Administration
subfiles.to: Provincial governors of Taiwan
subfiles.about: Orders stronger enforcement against unlicensed vessels and clarifies that the 21° licensing line is not the Philippine boundary.
subfiles.summary: The circular complains that controls remained incomplete and that unlicensed fishing vessels were still frequently reported. It explains that the 21° line was selected to prevent shipwrecks and international disputes, not to define the Philippine boundary, and names Yami and North Island as Philippine territory north of that latitude. Governors are instructed to publicize that Taiwan’s regulation never applies within another country’s territorial waters.

subfiles.title: Hull informs Dern of Taiwan’s boundary clarification
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.to: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Forwards despatch No. 53 and explains the outcome of Ketcham’s negotiations with Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that Taiwan declined to amend General Order No. 33. Nevertheless, its acting administrative director sent letters to all provincial governors explicitly indicating that 21° north was not the northern boundary of the Philippines. A copy of Ketcham’s February 21 despatch is enclosed.

subfiles.title: War Department acknowledges the final Taiwan report
subfiles.from: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull, Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the State Department’s final report and transmits it to the acting Philippine governor-general.
subfiles.summary: The War Department confirms receipt of Hull’s April 1 letter and Ketcham’s despatch No. 53. It notes that the materials have been reviewed and that copies were forwarded to the Acting Governor-General of the Philippine Islands.

interest: The file offers an unusually detailed view of how a seemingly technical fisheries regulation became a question of sovereignty and international relations. It combines specifications for vessel markings, logbooks, tonnage, and crew qualifications with a candid Philippine intelligence assessment of illicit fishing, trade, resource extraction, arrests, and the practical weakness of maritime patrols. The sequence also documents a revealing diplomatic compromise: Taiwan refused to amend the regulation or purport to define another power’s boundary, but formally acknowledged that Philippine territory extended north of the licensing line. The duplicate and enclosed copies make the bundle useful for tracing how information moved among colonial Taiwan, Manila, Tokyo, and Washington; notably, despite the file title’s reference to sponges, the surviving documents concern motor fishing craft and other marine activities rather than sponge fishing specifically.
